source: Kulkarni and Simon (1988) The processes of scientific discovery: the strategy of experimentation (CMU full-text copy), Holmes's account of Krebs
finding: The paper paraphrases Holmes's reconstruction (notebooks plus interviews) in three segments. Segment 1, 26 July to 15 November 1931: tissue-slice tests of amino acids, mostly negative, then the ornithine surprise. Segment 2, 15 Nov to about 14 Jan 1932: Krebs checked derivatives of ornithine, none worked, effect looked specific. Segment 3, 14 Jan to 13 April: new apparatus, ammonia shown to be the nitrogen source by 23 Jan, ornithine judged a catalyst, arginase link, citrulline.
numbers: Surprise came after about 3.5 months of work (26 Jul to 15 Nov 1931). Interpreting and testing took about 5 more months. About 4 weeks were spent on known ammonia-to-urea facts first. Krebs thought for two weeks about the arginase link. 13 April 1932 test: 24.5 molecules of urea per molecule of ornithine. Citrulline test 25 April, first paper out about 30 April.
quote: the cycle might have occurred to Krebs ... in the manner of gestalt switch
limits: Secondhand: this is Kulkarni and Simon quoting Holmes, not Holmes 1980 or the notebooks. No count of individual experiments is given. Logs give no reason why ornithine was tested on 15 Nov; the ornithine run was a departure from the current line.
agent_relevance: Real order: routine verification, then broad screen, then one anomaly, then scope check by derivatives, then quantitative mechanism, then literature link. The surprise was a rare event inside a long routine stretch.

source: Kulkarni and Simon (1988) The processes of scientific discovery: the strategy of experimentation (CMU full-text copy), KEKADA rules
finding: KEKADA is a production system with surprise-focus rules. Rule 2: if an outcome violates its expectation, note a surprise and make it the focus of attention. Rule 4: if the surprise may lie in a subprocess, study that subprocess. Rule 5: if it may be common to a class of substances, study the scope. Expectations come from the mean of prior outcomes with a tolerance band, or from a preset prior value when no prior run exists. Hypotheses carry counters: failure, failed-effort, implied-failure.
numbers: 3 expectation rules; 5 problem-proposer heuristics; 3 sets of choice rules (processes, substances, hypotheses). Hypothesis-modifier rules are absent in this version.
limits: Hand-written for one case (Krebs). The expectation prior and many facts are supplied by the authors.
agent_relevance: This is the only explicit surprise-driven operator order on record: expect, compare, focus on the violation, propose subprocess or scope study, count failed effort. It can be written as a prompt rule.

source: Kulkarni and Simon (1988) The processes of scientific discovery: the strategy of experimentation (CMU full-text copy), what KEKADA reproduced and where it did not
finding: KEKADA rediscovered the ornithine cycle in three scenarios that differ in when catalysis is considered. Scenario 1: catalysis not considered until data point to it. Scenario 2: considered early but ranked low. Scenario 3: considered very likely from the start, which the authors call unlikely because it does not explain Krebs's two weeks of puzzlement. Steps marked by an asterisk were chosen by the user, not the program, for example citrulline as intermediate and which source of nitrogen to test.
numbers: No match fraction is reported. In the text I counted about 10 asterisk (user-decided) steps across scenarios, including the final citrulline step. Three scenarios. Divergences listed in section 5: the alanine surprise, Krebs's doubt about the tissue-slice method, cyanate and pyrimidine ideas, and the slow route to the cyclic path.
quote: the discovery appears as a gradual development, the steps connected in a logical order
limits: Partial reproduction only. The program was interactive. The authors state it is not known why Krebs ran the ornithine test then, nor why the cycle took so long after catalysis was known. They say the alanine surprise perhaps makes the sequence appear more logical and determinate than it was. No independent replication of KEKADA was found.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 2: no quantified step match exists. Honest reading: KEKADA matches the coarse order (surprise, scope, mechanism) and partly fits the late stage, with human help at the hardest steps. Do not claim a measured fit.

source: Kulkarni and Simon (1988) The processes of scientific discovery: the strategy of experimentation (CMU full-text copy), Holmes's remark and the surprise caveat
finding: Holmes said he once expected a gestalt switch, but the reconstruction shows a gradual path. Kulkarni and Simon warn that the surprise at the low alanine yield was probably not felt by Krebs, who simply kept testing amino acids. Reading surprise into early steps may impose tidy order after the fact.
numbers: Two-week puzzlement over the arginase link; about 4 weeks on known ammonia work; 3.5 months before the anomaly.
limits: Authors' own judgment, not a measurement.
agent_relevance: A rule that fires on every deviation would over-trigger. The real surprise was one large departure (urea about double the expected rate with ornithine plus ammonia). Use a threshold on the size of the miss.

source: Grasshoff and May (2003) Hans Krebs's and Kurt Henseleit's laboratory notebooks and their discovery of the urea cycle, reconstructed with computer models (in Reworking the Bench)
finding: Only the publisher landing page and reference list were reachable; the chapter text is behind a paywall. References show the group's earlier source work: Bern Studies 2000 (Zur Theorie des Experiments) and 2001 (two volumes of notebook documents for Krebs and Henseleit), plus Grasshoff 1995 on the methodological function of surprises.
numbers: Chapter pp. 269-294; 8 citations listed by the site.
limits: No step counts or sequence were readable. Gap 1 detail from this source stays open.
agent_relevance: Grasshoff treats surprise as a method step, which matches KEKADA, but we have no measured numbers from it.

source: Dunbar (1997) How scientists think; Dunbar and Fugelsang (2004-05) causal thinking and the unexpected
finding: Reachable records confirm the works exist (Dunbar and Fugelsang 2005, Neuropsychologia 43; 2004 chapter on how scientists and students interpret the unexpected). No full text was opened, so no rate of unexpected findings is verified here.
limits: The often-quoted figure that about half of lab-meeting findings were unexpected is memory only. Do not cite it as a number.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open. The claim to carry is qualitative: labs first suspect method, then change the model.

source: Panchekha (blog) Can an LLM reproduce Kepler from raw data
finding: One-person test on synthetic Kepler-style data (Earth and Mars like planets, 30 years). ChatGPT Pro reasoned 67 minutes, found periodicities, noticed a 2.1 second overlap but did not pursue it, and ended with a rotating-ray or breathing-orbit model, not ellipses. Codex with larger hints stayed at epicycles. Author: Kepler remains undefeated.
numbers: About 15,000 daily observations at 0.001 degree (about 10x Tycho accuracy); 67 min for the first run; 41 more minutes of self-assessment. One trial each.
limits: Blog, n=1, synthetic data, read through a page summariser. No scoring against a record. Order was compared by eye: Ptolemy-like then Copernicus-like, not Kepler order.
agent_relevance: Confirms there is still no scored replay-of-history test. It also shows the useful failure: the model noticed the right clue and dropped it.

source: Agarwal et al. (2026 v3) AutoDiscovery: open-ended scientific discovery via Bayesian surprise
finding: Uses Bayesian surprise (shift in LLM belief before and after an experiment) as the search reward. MCTS with progressive widening, fixed budget of 500 hypothesis evaluations, same GPT-4o discovery agent in every arm. Tree searches beat repeated sampling and linear search; MCTS gave 5-29% more surprising discoveries than strong search baselines, and was best on 17 of 21 datasets.
numbers: 21 datasets; 500 evaluations per run; human study over 500+ hypotheses: 67% of surprising discoveries were also surprising to experts; Bayesian surprise correlated 67% with human surprisal, higher than other rewards.
limits: Surprise is used to pick which branch to expand, not to force an explanation before moving on. Equal budget is a count of evaluations, not tokens. Surprise is judged by the same LLM family.
agent_relevance: Nearest 2020-2026 test of the KEKADA idea: surprise as the signal that directs search, at equal budget. Gap 3 partly closed: surprise-driven search works; the explain-before-moving-on part is untested.

source: Agarwal et al. (2026) AutoDiscovery, greedy vs MCTS, appendix reasoning-model run
finding: Greedy tree search (MCTS with exploration constant 0) is a controlled greedy baseline. With GPT-4o, search efficiency of greedy and beam declines over time while MCTS holds. With the reasoning model o4-mini, MCTS and greedy show no difference at 500 hypotheses.
numbers: Budget 500; greedy and MCTS equal under o4-mini; authors say a drop-off is likely at larger budgets (footnote 7).
limits: Only two model families; the reason given (fewer duplicate experiments) is a conjecture.
agent_relevance: Greedy anchoring costs something for weaker models over long runs and little for reasoning models at this length. A no-repeat rule matters more for non-reasoning backbones.

source: Toledo et al. (2025) AI research agents for machine learning: search, exploration and generalization in MLE-bench
finding: Controlled comparison of selection policy and operator set. With AIDE operators, swapping greedy for MCTS or evolutionary search gave no gain; sweeping the MCTS exploration constant over 0, 0.25, 0.75 changed medal rates only marginally. Better operators did help: AIRA greedy 45.5% vs AIDE greedy 39.8% (14% relative). With better operators MCTS (R1) reached 47%.
numbers: MLE-bench Lite, 20 seeds, 24 hour window; AIDE memory on vs off: nearly identical medal rates; AIRA operators use about 2x completion tokens; best result 39.6% to 47.7% medal rate; validation score kept rising while held-out test plateaued or fell.
limits: Operator prompts changed together (complexity cue, scoped memory, think tokens), so no single-part ablation. Token use is not equal across arms.
agent_relevance: Search-level exploration rules (MCTS, exploration constant) did not beat greedy unless operators changed. For our agent, fix the operators first. Also: a memory of past tries added nothing on its own.

source: Toledo et al. (2025) AIRA operators: scoped memory of siblings and of the debug chain
finding: For draft and improve, memory returns only sibling attempts of the node, to push diversity. For debug, memory returns the full chain of earlier fix attempts to avoid undo-redo loops. A complexity cue rises with the number of children: minimal under 2, moderate 2 to 3, advanced at 5 or more.
numbers: Complexity thresholds as above; part of the operator set that gave 45.5% vs 39.8%.
limits: Not ablated alone. This is the closest thing found to a rule that shows past failed attempts to the next attempt.
agent_relevance: A usable form of the impasse rule: show the model its sibling failures and the debug chain, and raise the demanded size of change after repeated tries.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: language agents with verbal reinforcement learning
finding: Ablations of the explain-after-failure step. HotPotQA with ground-truth context: adding episodic memory of the last trajectory helps; adding a written self-reflection gives a further 8 points absolute. HumanEval Rust, 50 hardest problems, GPT-4: base 0.60, no test generation 0.52, no self-reflection 0.60, full Reflexion 0.68.
numbers: 100 HotPotQA questions; 50 Rust problems; retries until 3 consecutive failures on HotPotQA.
limits: Small samples, single run, tests from the environment supply the outcome signal. Not equal tokens: reflection adds calls. Ground-truth context in the HotPotQA ablation.
agent_relevance: Best controlled evidence that writing an explanation after an outcome helps, but only with an external test result (G: external signal). Dropping the explanation removed the whole gain.

source: Tsui (2026, COLM) Self-Correction Bench: uncovering the self-correction blind spot
finding: Same injected error, shown as user-attributed or model-attributed. 14 open non-reasoning models fix their own error far less often: average blind spot 64.5%. Closed models: Claude 3.5 Haiku 52.5%, Sonnet 4 41.4%. Reasoning models show a small, even negative blind spot. Appending Wait cuts the blind spot 89.3%.
numbers: Wait on non-thinking models, mean accuracy: DeepSeek-V3-0324 0.567 to 0.902 (R1-0528 0.908); Qwen3-14B 0.117 to 0.868 (thinking 0.843); Qwen3-32B 0.045 to 0.793 (0.894); phi-4 0.325 to 0.701 (0.707). SFT with 5,306 correction traces cut the blind spot 76.0%. Non-math domains 62.8%.
limits: Errors are injected, not found without feedback, so this is a different question from Huang et al. Wait also lengthens output, so tokens are not equal.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 10 in part: reasoning models do correct their own mistakes in-context, the weakness is activation, and a cheap Wait cue restores it. Huang's finding still describes plain chat models.

source: Huang et al. (2024) vs newer reasoning models: status of the 2023 intrinsic self-correction result
finding: The 2023 numbers (GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 in round 1; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0) were on GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. No 2025-26 paper that repeats the exact Huang protocol (no oracle, same prompt) on o-series or R1-class models with numbers was located. Tsui (d13) is the nearest evidence.
numbers: Huang: GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5, 91.5, 89.0 over rounds (from the earlier re-opened paper, evidence b21).
limits: Absence of a located replication, found with search tools throttled; not proof none exists. This line itself is a negative-search note.
agent_relevance: Keep G (check against external signal) as a rule. For reasoning backbones let the model self-check inside one chain, but do not add a separate unaided critique round.

source: Gap note: Gruber on Darwin, notebook timeline from reachable sources
finding: Reachable secondary summary: Notebook B began mid-July 1837 with the first tree sketch on page 36; C by February 1838; D and M started in the Shrewsbury summer of 1838; E holds a 2 December 1838 entry; M has about 60 pages on moral and social behaviour. Darwin began Malthus in late September 1838 and noted the insight on 28 September 1838. So selection came about 14 months after notebook B opened.
numbers: About 14 months from B (July 1837) to Malthus (28 Sept 1838); tree sketch on B page 36; M about 60 pages.
limits: Wikipedia, not Gruber. No per-topic entry counts, no parallel-stream counts, and the article does not discuss Kohn, Schweber or Ospovat. Gruber's own tallies stay unread.
agent_relevance: Darwin's path had several streams in parallel (transmutation, man, mind) and a trigger from reading outside the field, not from a failed experiment. Order: fact-find, branching structure, an outside idea (Malthus), then breeder analogy in December.

source: Gap note: reliability of reconstructions (Nickelsen and Grasshoff 2009; Holmes 1980)
finding: The Springer landing page for Nickelsen and Grasshoff, Concepts from the Bench (2009), was reachable but not the text. No measured agreement between independent reconstructions of one notebook was found. The one comparison available in opened text is Holmes (gradual path, interview-informed) against KEKADA (logical order, user help), which differ on when catalysis was considered.
limits: Closed text. Holmes 1980 (Fed Proc 39) also not opened.
agent_relevance: Treat any reconstructed order as one reading. Test our agent against its own logged order, not a historian's.
